 JAKARTA, KOMPAS.com - The National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) has reported that there are 253 districts/cities vulnerable to flooding and 202 districts/cities at risk of landslides based on historical data.
 This announcement is made in preparation for hydrometeorological disasters as the rainy season 2026/2027 approaches.
 “There are 253 districts/cities prone to flooding and 202 districts/cities vulnerable to landslides, with an approximate 113.8 million people at risk of being affected,” said the Acting Head of the BNPB Center for Data, Information, and Disaster Communication, Berton SP Panjaitan, in a press release on the official BNPB website on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).
 Berton explained that the peak of the rainy season is expected to vary across regions. For instance, Sumatra is projected to face its peak in December 2026 and January 2027.
 Meanwhile, Java is anticipated to see peak rains in January and February 2027, while Kalimantan may have its peak in January and March 2027.
 Berton noted that other regions must also adjust their preparedness based on their local rainy season characteristics.
 “To mitigate the impacts of disasters, local governments are encouraged to establish and activate the rainy season action plans by November. Contingency plans should be updated, taking into account impact scenarios, inter-agency role distributions, activation triggers, evacuation routes, and resource availability,” he explained.
 In addition, logistical readiness must be checked to ensure that the needs of refugees can be met.
 He also reminded that early warning systems need to be tested down to the village level. Meanwhile, posts, rubber boats, rapid response teams, monitoring of water levels, and public kitchens should be prepared before the peak of the rainy season.
 “Special attention is also required for slopes affected by forest fires, particularly in East Java and Central Java. Monitoring since the start of the rainy season is vital to anticipate the potential for flash floods and landslides,” Berton stated.
 BNPB urged local governments and the public to enhance their preparedness for forest fires and hydrometeorological disasters.
 He encouraged communities in vulnerable areas to stay informed about weather forecasts and early warnings from official sources, avoid activities that might trigger fires, conserve clean water, and promptly report any disaster incidents to local authorities.
 “Early preparedness, cross-sector coordination, and community participation are essential parts of reducing disaster risks and impacts,” Berton concluded.
